title: Never After Dark: A Terrifying New Twist on a Haunted House Tale
excerpt: We love a horror movie that looks at four different genres and says, "Yes."
content:
Never After Dark is the title of a very good horror film, and also the rule that main character/roaming freelance exorcist Airi (Moeka Hoshi) lives by: after dark, the spirits of the dead become much stronger, and trying to convince them to move on becomes ever more dangerous. During the day, with the right tools and the right rites, she can, usually, gently, guide the restless departed on to their next chapter.

The important thing to notice here is that it is gentle. Airi is comfortable with the dead. She doesn’t approach them as anything scary or menacing—her job is a work of healing. One of the reasons for that is her companion on her travels: the ghost of her big sister, Miku (Kurumi Inagaki), still appearing as a teenager years after her death, who, also gently, nudges Airi to focus more on the living than the dead. Their dynamic feels comfortable, teasing, lived-in, if you’ll pardon the expression. Or at least that’s the case until Airi pulls up to their latest gig, and our story begins.  

I often say on this website that nothing scares me. And, well, that might be a slight exaggeration because, for whatever reason, Japanese horror often scares me. This movie might have, slightly, a little bit, scared me.

She’s hired to deal with a ghost in an old hotel that’s now being used as a private home. The woman who hired her, Teiko (Tae Kimura) is a recent widow with an adult son, but she’s very much a rich, stylish, almost bubbly woman who looks and acts at least a decade younger than she is. Underneath her cheerful exterior, however, is a real pathos—her husband hasn’t been gone long. She’s trying to figure out how to live as a widow, and she desperately wants proof of an afterlife. (It’s never said explicitly, but I assume she wants to know that her husband is OK, on a deep cosmic level.) Meanwhile her son Gunji (Kento Kako), makes a point of saying he “doesn’t believe in any of this stuff” to Airi during their first meeting. He’s openly skeptical of her, worried she’s scamming his mom, and frustrated that they have to stay somewhere else during the exorcism. (The fact that he also thinks Airi is cute, and wants to get to know her better, only becomes a snag later on in the film.)

It’s a classic haunted house set up that doesn’t go in any of the typical directions. Airi is legit, and we know she’s legit from the first scene. Gunji is blustering and borderline rude about his own agnosticism toward ghosts, but he’s also a nice guy who genuinely likes Airi. Teiko seems like a flibbertigibbet, but she wants to help Airi in her work, and her interest in the paranormal is sincere. And then plot goes in some fascinating directions, and I—who have seen A LOT of haunted house films—was struck by a few things that felt genuinely new.

This is the debut feature from director Dave Boyle, who has worked in Japan for years, and previously made House of Ninjas for Netflix. (Tae Kimura and Kento Kako were both in House of Ninjas, and Boyle and Kako have now formed a production company, Signal181, Inc.) Here, Boyle has mashed up the Western Gothic, J-Horror, and a haunted hotel-turned-home that feels like The Overlook’s more elegant sister.

As there often is in this kind of a story, there is a deep-rooted trauma in Airi’s past. But she’s had it for a long time, it’s part of her, and as we gradually learn the details, it’s clear that this was a thing that could actually happen to someone in her line of work, not a writer working backwards through an idea to come up with something “shocking”. The past and present bump into each other and collapse repeatedly over the course of the film, just like the dead and the living. (I also want to give a moment to praise Mutsuo Yoshioka’s performance, in a role I’d rather not spoil.)

The house and its grounds are a gorgeous work of set design and atmosphere. Airi walks through the house to familiarize herself with it, but also to give us a classic haunted house tour, so that as each new twist unfolds, deep shadows, sheet-draped furniture, and inexplicably open doors become terrifying. When the horror elements bubble up, the makeup and special effects are practical, and beautiful. Here, Boyle worked with a pair of legends: production designer Yuji Hayashida and special effects makeup artist Tomo Hyakutake. Boyle has spoken in interviews about his love of all-time-classic The Changeling, and you can feel the inspiration here—he captures a similar feeling of grief and horror, but also a deep, deep empathy for his characters.

The mechanics of Airi’s work as an exorcist are beautifully presented. Again, I don’t want to spoil anything, but I especially don’t want to spoil the tools of the exorcism themselves. They’re so simple and elegant that as I watched Airi use them, I couldn’t believe I’d never seen anything quite like them before. Airi is one of the most instantly lovable main characters I’ve ever seen in a film, and she just gets more compelling as the film goes on—there are extended scenes where she has to kill a lot of hours until it’s safe to try her ritual, and she fills those by swilling beer, dancing to fantastic pop from clipping.’s Jonathan Snipes, and arguing with Gunji about Kraftwerk.  

I saw Never After Dark last month, as part of Film at Lincoln Center’s Scary Movies XIII, a festival that is, as the name suggests, full of scary movies. I saw several films there, and actually liked all of them for different reasons. (I’ve already reviewed Buddy, and I’ll probably write more about that film later this fall; I’m waiting for two others to be released before I talk about them.) Of all of them, though, this is the one that I’ve thought about the most. It’s on a shelf next to Hokum and Widow’s Bay in my head, and as we hurtle toward the end of this year Hokum and Widow’s Bay still stand as two of my favorite things.

Never After Dark is about something, but not in a cliched way of like “this horror movie is about grief, or tech billionaires, or my relationship with my mom”—it’s more about how personal tragedy crashes into the meatgrinder of life. Airi has her own past that has shaped her present. When she comes to the Teiko’s home, the haunting that awaits her does not care about that. She comes in thinking she can use her usual rituals, and play by the rules of the spirit world, and then dust her hands off and go on to the next case. And honestly? If the movie had just been that I think it still would have been a fun, spooky haunted house story, because Boyle’s writing is sharp enough, the atmosphere so perfect, and, like I said, Airi is one of the best characters I’ve met all year. But instead, at a certain moment Airi discovers that this haunting is not normal, it’s not following the pattern that every other haunting has, and she’s in totally uncharted territory. And that’s when the movie goes from being just fun to being terrifying.

Nothing scares me. But… this one made me nervous. I maybe leaned forward. I may have clenched my fists a little.

Without spoiling the haunting, I’ll say that it’s really unusual, and adds a whole other genre element on top of the pure supernatural horror that I was expecting. It’s really unique, and I’m excited to write more about Never After Dark in a spoiler-filled piece where I can really dig into stuff. But for now, I’ll say that if you like Japanese Horror, gothics, haunted hotels, ghost stories, or exorcisms, you need to seek this one out. icon-paragraph-end
